Two-tier fixture strategy and its replay seam
SecurTxn Brand Identity System (glyph, palette, typography, a11y)
Swappable-implementation seams selected at the DI root

nodes.label: Real DigiLocker fixture tier
nodes.rationale: Captured from the live Sandbox API on 2026-09-08 so day-to-day development doesn't burn paid verification calls: every KYC call except /authenticate and /status is billable live, replaying is free.

nodes.label: Vendor test environment rejected
nodes.rationale: test-api.sandbox.co.in is a mock replayer answering only requests that exactly match examples in a forked Postman collection; no DigiLocker examples exist on the account so every DigiLocker call 404s (verified 2026-09-08, including with payloads copied verbatim from vendor docs). Even working, it would return canned data, never a real signed document.

nodes.label: World ID Selfie Check fixtures
nodes.rationale: Two real sandbox verifications captured 2026-09-09 so tests can replay the flow without a phone, a camera, or the World verifier being reachable — same purpose as fixtures/digilocker/, but committed.

nodes.label: Sanctions interface with MVP stub
nodes.rationale: Shipped as an interface plus stub so the decision engine can depend on a screening step before a real provider is contracted.

nodes.label: Evidence chain viewer
nodes.rationale: Shows the break point when the chain is invalid rather than a generic failure, so an auditor can localise tampering.

nodes.label: Pure decision state machine
nodes.rationale: decision/ and evidence/chain.ts are deliberately pure with no DB or network imports, so the two things that must be auditable are testable in isolation.

nodes.label: Confirmed Payee + Exception Desk
nodes.rationale: A control layer in front of stablecoin custodians because the most expensive failure in crypto B2B payments is sending money to the wrong wallet irrecoverably; pre-send verification beats detect-and-refund.

nodes.label: System architecture (web / api / bridge / CRE / contracts / Hedera)
nodes.norm_label: system architecture (web / api / bridge / cre / contracts / hedera)
nodes.rationale: approval-bridge runs on the approver's local machine because it is the only process with USB access to the Ledger; apps/api never talks to the device directly.

nodes.label: Progress checklist
nodes.rationale: A box is ticked only after its unit test passes, so the document cannot drift into optimism; structure-only tasks are ticked by hand and noted inline, and a parent stays unticked until every child is ticked.

nodes.label: Non-negotiable design principles
nodes.rationale: Stated as absolute so convenience cannot win an argument: a change violating one is wrong regardless of how convenient it is.

nodes.label: Gap: vendor-level events have no evidence chain
nodes.norm_label: gap: vendor-level events have no evidence chain
nodes.rationale: EvidenceRecord requires a paymentRequestId, so identity-verified, wallet-confirmed and KYB-status-changed events are unrecorded; needs either a nullable payment reference or a separate vendor chain.

nodes.label: Monorepo structure (pnpm workspaces, TypeScript everywhere)
nodes.rationale: Every external SDK in scope is npm/TS-native, so there is no reason to introduce a second language anywhere in the stack.

nodes.label: canonicalize() deterministic JSON
nodes.rationale: JSON.stringify preserves insertion order, which is not guaranteed across engines and versions, so two equal payloads built differently would hash differently.

nodes.label: lib/canonical-json.ts key ordering rule
nodes.rationale: Keys sorted by code unit, array order preserved, undefined dropped, and anything JSON cannot round-trip rejected outright; hashes stored as bare 64-hex so every link including the all-zero genesis has the same shape.

nodes.label: Chain verification on read (content vs linkage break)
nodes.norm_label: chain verification on read (content vs linkage break)
nodes.rationale: Recomputed from genesis on every read rather than trusting a stored flag, reporting the first break with its index and distinguishing a payload that no longer hashes to its stored hash from a record that does not link to its predecessor.

nodes.label: evidence_accessed self-audit event
nodes.rationale: Reading the audit trail is itself audited; appendStandalone is the one non-transactional append and retries on a unique-constraint collision because two concurrent readers can race for the same chain tip.

nodes.label: EvidencePayload envelope
nodes.rationale: The union is closed and discriminated so a payload whose data does not match its eventType is rejected rather than written, and Zod strips undeclared keys so a leaked field does not survive parsing. Where the doc and the Zod schemas disagree, the schemas win.

nodes.label: payee_consent evidence event
nodes.rationale: Ordered before match and decision because it authorises them: a chain showing a match with no consent ahead of it describes a system with no gate. The consent signature stays on the PayeeConsent row, since a second copy in an anchored structure buys nothing a dispute needs.

nodes.label: vendor_match evidence event
nodes.rationale: Kept as a separate record from decision, in causal order: one combined record would lose the distinction between 'the match was wrong' and 'the policy was wrong'.

nodes.label: B2 HCS evidence anchoring + Merkle layer
nodes.norm_label: b2 hcs evidence anchoring + merkle layer
nodes.rationale: Leaves prefixed 0x00 and nodes 0x01 so a node cannot pose as a leaf; odd nodes are promoted not duplicated, because duplication lets two leaf sets collide on one root; proof pairs are never sorted because position is what the proof claims. Anchoring counts as done only once a mirror node serves the root back.

nodes.label: Evidence hash chain
nodes.rationale: Every state-changing write inserts a record in the same transaction, linked to its predecessor's hash, so insertion, removal or edit is detectable on read.

nodes.label: Principle 3 — every state change produces an evidence record
nodes.norm_label: principle 3 — every state change produces an evidence record
nodes.rationale: An action is not complete until its record is appended to the hash chain, so the audit trail cannot lag behind reality.

nodes.label: Check 1 — XMLDSig signature verification
nodes.rationale: Parsing the XML without verifying the signature throws away the entire security property — an unverified XML is just a text file.

nodes.label: Same-transaction append rule
nodes.rationale: EvidenceService.append takes a transaction client precisely so there is deliberately no 'append later' method.

nodes.label: decision/ and evidence/chain.ts are pure
nodes.rationale: The two things that must be auditable have no DB or network imports, so they are testable in isolation.

nodes.label: decide() decision engine state machine
nodes.rationale: Written as one explicit pure function rather than scattered if/else so every branch is auditable and testable by direct input injection; hard blocks are ordered before soft ones and first match wins.

nodes.label: GET /internal/identity-registry/:address hook
nodes.rationale: The real integration point: it makes the platform's own KYC data the compliance backend that ATS's ERC-3643 mode calls out to, rather than a cosmetic add-on.

nodes.label: Vendor model
nodes.rationale: digilockerUserId is the identity primary key, never the Aadhaar number: receiving a full Aadhaar number would create Data Vault obligations this flow otherwise avoids.

nodes.label: VendorWallet model
nodes.rationale: controlProofSig proves wallet custody only, never that the signer represents the named legal entity, so it is never alone sufficient for CONFIRMED.

nodes.label: VerificationTier (TIER0-TIER3)
nodes.rationale: Tier gates the decision engine: a high-value payment to a liveness-only payee must return REVERIFY, and thresholds live in config because different customers set different risk appetites.

nodes.label: P7 decision engine gates
nodes.rationale: Sanctions, duplicate invoice, wallet CONFIRMED, tier ceiling, freshness (DigiLocker TTL, credential expiry, 90-day selfie window) and on-chain KYC granted.

nodes.label: P3/P4 payee notification and EIP-712 consent
nodes.norm_label: p3/p4 payee notification and eip-712 consent
nodes.rationale: DENY terminates with no match run and no funds moved; ACCEPT is signed by the CONFIRMED wallet with amount, token and invoiceRef inside the signed payload. runDecision refuses without an ACCEPTED consent, enforced in the service rather than by convention (D63), and the consent route is deliberately unauthenticated because the signature is the authorisation.

nodes.label: ComplianceGateway / AtsComplianceGateway
nodes.rationale: grantKyc carries a credential reference and no PII; Hedera ids resolve to EVM addresses via the mirror node rather than long-zero derivation, and a reverted grant is an error not a success. The read was verified to discriminate against a live bond, which is the only thing that makes it a control rather than a constant.

nodes.label: VerifiableCredential model + lib/vc.ts
nodes.rationale: Credential body stays off-chain with the chain holding only a reference; expiresAt derives from aadhaarKycTtl and usable is computed on read, never cached, and an absent TTL becomes a far-future date rather than 0.

nodes.label: registryVerifiedContact independent-channel callback control
nodes.rationale: An attacker submitting a real company's name and tax ID with their own wallet and phone would confirm their own fraud if the callback dialled the submitted number, so the contact comes only from an independent registry lookup or a contact on file predating the change — never the current submission. Seed data hardcodes one so the real control logic still executes in demos.

nodes.label: Check 3 — same-subject linkage
nodes.rationale: The DigiLocker user id appears in both the PAN Person uid and the Aadhaar KycRes txn string; asserting equality is what proves the two documents describe one person.

nodes.label: Check 4 — KYC TTL enforcement
nodes.rationale: CONFIRMED is time-bounded, not permanent: the observed KycRes ttl is issue + 1 year, so re-verification is scheduled before expiry.

nodes.label: Consent gates verification, and verification gates money
nodes.norm_label: consent gates verification, and verification gates money
nodes.rationale: Nothing is verified until the receiver agrees to be verified, and no money moves until verification passes — verifying after settlement is detect-and-refund, which banks already do. Consent is also the primary throttle, because each probe costs the victim's active acceptance.

nodes.label: container.ts DI root
nodes.rationale: The only place a swappable implementation is chosen, so provider substitution (mock vs live identity provider, fallback vs CRE vendor matcher) never leaks into call sites.

nodes.label: api-client.ts sole network surface
nodes.rationale: Nothing here imports @cp/api; it talks over HTTP only, keeping the two dependency trees disjoint.

nodes.label: Approver-scoped token
nodes.rationale: Rejected on POST /payments/:id/propose (§4.2) so the signer role can never also author a proposal — role separation enforced by token scope.

nodes.label: vendorMatch interface
nodes.rationale: The only thing apps/api imports, so neither the in-process fallback nor the TEE workflow is visible to callers.

nodes.label: @cp/api core platform
nodes.rationale: Single Fastify service holding vendor registry, decision engine, evidence hash-chain and exception desk; deliberately excludes any signing capability so that the blast radius of a compromised cloud process stops at proposals.

nodes.label: @cp/approval-bridge
nodes.rationale: Separate app with its own dependency tree rather than a module inside @cp/api, because the isolation between proposing and signing must be architectural, not a code-path convention (§0 principle 5).

nodes.label: @cp/web AP dashboard
nodes.rationale: Components are grouped by domain, mirroring the api's module slices, so a change to one domain touches one folder on each side.

nodes.label: @cp/cre-workflows
nodes.rationale: Confidential vendor matching, delivered as two implementations of one interface with match scoring shared between them.

nodes.label: pnpm workspace package globs
nodes.rationale: Two globs, apps/* and packages/*, define the monorepo: separate apps are what makes the api / approval-bridge isolation an installable boundary.

nodes.label: API process never signs
nodes.rationale: The API only writes proposals. Only apps/approval-bridge, on the approver's machine, can move funds, gated by on-device Clear Signing (docs/architecture.md §0 principle 1, §4.3).

nodes.label: Vertical slice module layout
nodes.rationale: Modules are vertical slices rather than a shared routes/ + services/ split: each domain's HTTP surface, business logic and validation live together, and cross-module calls go through a service, never through another module's routes.

nodes.label: Approver-local-only execution
nodes.rationale: Runs on the approver's local machine, never in cloud infrastructure: it is the only process with USB access to the Ledger and therefore the only thing that can move money.

nodes.label: UI approval writes a proposal only
nodes.norm_label: ui approval writes a proposal only
nodes.rationale: Approving in the UI does not send money; the send happens on the approver's machine via the Ledger (§4.3).

nodes.label: Fallback as reference implementation
nodes.rationale: The fallback is not throwaway: it is the reference implementation the CRE version is tested against, and the reason Phases 1-4 are not blocked on enrollment (§8). It runs in-process with no enclave and no access gate.

nodes.label: World ID Selfie Check (approver second factor)
nodes.norm_label: world id selfie check (approver second factor)
nodes.rationale: Proves a real distinct human independently of the specific hardware key holder that Clear Signing proves. Medium assurance only, so UI copy must say 'a live human confirmed this action', never 'identity verified'.

nodes.label: P2 sender World ID check, every payment
nodes.norm_label: p2 sender world id check, every payment
nodes.rationale: Signal = paymentId and the proof must match the sender's enrolment nullifier, so a live continuous human is provably the one raising this specific payment; enforced in the service, since request-consent refuses without it (D64).

nodes.label: B4 World ID Selfie Check integration
nodes.norm_label: b4 world id selfie check integration
nodes.rationale: UNIQUE (nullifier, action, signal) deliberately replaces the documented UNIQUE (nullifier, action), which would let each human approve exactly one payment ever. The nullifier is stored as Decimal(78,0) because field elements come back unpadded and text storage would make one person look like two. Signal binding is compared against hashSignal(expected) because the v4 verifier is never told which signal was expected, and our own clock is stored rather than upstream created_at.

nodes.label: Track C — wiring the sponsor integrations into the flow
nodes.norm_label: track c — wiring the sponsor integrations into the flow
nodes.rationale: Three integrations were built and verified against real services yet none was load-bearing at runtime, which is a stated disqualifier; the goal of the track is that one payment cannot complete without passing through all of them.

nodes.label: World ID / Selfie Check integration feedback
nodes.norm_label: world id / selfie check integration feedback
nodes.rationale: The protocol behaved exactly as documented; the cost was in undocumented behaviour and in one check that silently moved from World's side to the integrator's. Raw captures are kept in fixtures/worldid/ so every claim is reproducible rather than remembered. Being told plainly that Selfie Check is medium assurance is what let the control be placed where it holds.

nodes.label: onboardingSessionNonce session binding
nodes.rationale: Each check can individually pass while belonging to different people — an attacker can pair a borrowed genuine KYC session with their own wallet signature. An identical nonce across the liveness check, the document check and the wallet-control signature chains legal identity -> live face -> wallet key into one subject instead of three independent facts.

nodes.label: Assurance boundaries — do not overclaim
nodes.rationale: Selfie Check is medium assurance and proves the same human as enrolled, never which human; EIP-712 proves key possession, not personhood; DigiLocker proves legal identity, only as fresh as its TTL.

nodes.label: created_at is first-seen, not verified-at
nodes.rationale: Two runs hours apart returned an identical created_at, because it timestamps when the nullifier was first ever observed; persisting it as the verification time would have put a wrong timestamp in an audit record.

nodes.label: No way to read whether Selfie Check is enabled for an app
nodes.norm_label: no way to read whether selfie check is enabled for an app
nodes.rationale: No Portal or MCP field reports which credentials an app may request, so the gate that decides whether the integration works at all is invisible to the API describing the app; it was resolved only by building the whole integration and running it — an expensive way to discover a boolean.

nodes.label: Legacy presets can return a different credential than requested
nodes.norm_label: legacy presets can return a different credential than requested
nodes.rationale: Legacy presets return the maximum credential a user has, so selfieCheckLegacy can return an Orb credential and any policy keyed on identifier === 'selfie' rejects your strongest users.

nodes.label: Verifier returns success:true on a replayed nullifier
nodes.norm_label: verifier returns success:true on a replayed nullifier
nodes.rationale: HTTP 200 with reuse noted only inside a prose message string, so an integrator gating on success — the obvious thing to gate on — has no replay protection at all and no error to tell them.

nodes.label: UNIQUE (nullifier, action) is wrong for repeat actions
nodes.norm_label: unique (nullifier, action) is wrong for repeat actions
nodes.rationale: The nullifier is stable per person, so the documented constraint means each human can perform the action exactly once ever — and the failure looks like the control working correctly, so a team shipping the documented schema would find out in production. Scope uniqueness to the signal instead.

nodes.label: v4 signal verification moved to the integrator, silently
nodes.norm_label: v4 signal verification moved to the integrator, silently
nodes.rationale: v3 took the signal explicitly; the v4 endpoint takes only the IDKit payload, so success means 'valid for whatever signal_hash is inside it'. A genuine correctly-signed proof bound to any other context — or to the empty signal an unbound request produces — would have been recorded as authorising a specific payment with nothing looking wrong. Fix: compare responses[].signal_hash against hashSignal(expected) in the backend.

nodes.label: Field elements are unpadded hex
nodes.rationale: An observed merkle_root came back 63 hex characters in one run and 64 in the next, and nullifiers will be short roughly one time in sixteen, so string storage makes the same person look like two intermittently — breaking continuity for legitimate users and letting a replay through a UNIQUE index.

nodes.label: CRE TEE vendor-match workflow (cre.handlerInTee)
nodes.rationale: ConfidentialHTTPClient is deliberately not used — it lacks the TeeRuntime overload a TEE handler requires. Only the verdict crosses the enclave boundary, and the simulator is treated as logic verification only, never as a security demonstration.

nodes.label: FallbackVendorMatcher (non-confidential)
nodes.rationale: Built and wired first because it is what makes the whole pipeline demoable without waiting on CRE enrollment.

nodes.label: VendorMatcher interface
nodes.rationale: The decision engine is wired against the interface, not a concrete class, so swapping fallback for CRE is a one-line dependency-injection change.

nodes.label: P6 CRE confidential workflow (TEE digest comparison)
nodes.norm_label: p6 cre confidential workflow (tee digest comparison)
nodes.rationale: The enclave compares opaque digests so no plaintext identity ever enters it; NO_MATCH blocks and alerts the payee that someone claimed them and was wrong, which makes probing visible instead of silent.

nodes.label: evaluateMatch() shared match rule
nodes.rationale: Shared by the fallback, the TEE handler and the DON handler precisely so they cannot drift — if the fallback kept fuzzy scoring while CRE compared digests, the shared contract suite would stop proving anything about the CRE path.

nodes.label: B5 Chainlink CRE track
nodes.rationale: An earlier DEPLOYED-AND-ACTIVE claim was retracted: the gateway returned ACCEPTED while every execution failed in 0ms because confidential-workflows is a per-workflow entitlement not reported by cre whoami. Verdicts are now read off finished executions, never off the ACCEPTED response, and all four branches are proven because an always-MATCHED matcher would have looked identical on the happy path.

nodes.label: Principle 4 — confidential vendor matching runs in a TEE
nodes.norm_label: principle 4 — confidential vendor matching runs in a tee
nodes.rationale: Checks against vendor PII run inside the Chainlink CRE TEE handler rather than the main API process; a non-confidential fallback behind the same interface means the rest of the system does not care which is active.

nodes.label: The address is untrusted routing; the identity is the verification
nodes.norm_label: the address is untrusted routing; the identity is the verification
nodes.rationale: The sender pastes an address off an invoice — exactly where hijacking lives — and states who they intend to pay, so a tampered address is caught by being bound to a different DigiLocker subject.

nodes.label: Digest matching in the enclave (D62)
nodes.rationale: There is no crypto in the CRE enclave — node:crypto is banned by the SDK's restricted-modules list and no crypto.subtle global exists — so 'encrypt at rest, decrypt inside the enclave' has no primitive. Comparing HMAC digests as opaque bytes sidesteps it and the pepper never leaves the server. The cost is the near-miss band: exact-after-normalisation is stricter and defeats lookalike payees, but a reviewer can no longer tell a typo from a different company; a mismatch costs a retry, never money. One reason code for any identity mismatch, because per-field errors would give a prober a second bit.

nodes.label: Why invoice fraud fails
nodes.rationale: The sender can be fully tricked into pasting the attacker's address and still not lose the money, because the claimed PAN mismatches the address's KYC'd identity. To receive at all the attacker must complete DigiLocker KYC, so invoice fraud stops being free and anonymous and starts costing a real, traceable, prosecutable identity revocable across every buyer at once — structural, not a tunable policy. Escrow-as-deterrent and punitive deductions were deliberately rejected.

nodes.label: Open gap: the deployed CRE workflow predates D62
nodes.norm_label: open gap: the deployed cre workflow predates d62
nodes.rationale: The DON runs plaintext name scoring against a minScore the config schema no longer has, while the lookup endpoint now returns only digests, so flipping VENDOR_MATCHER to cre would make every payment a mismatch. Source and deployment are separate artefacts and a passing test suite says nothing about which one the DON is running.

nodes.label: Hedera ATS receivable tokenization
nodes.rationale: Control List, Pause and Lock modules are configured on deploy; the receivable is tokenized as a bond-like instrument only after the vendor is CONFIRMED and the decision permits sending.

nodes.label: ApprovalEvent model
nodes.rationale: selfieCheckProofRef holds an opaque reference to the stored IDKit result, not the raw proof.

nodes.label: P9-P11 HTLC lock / claim / refund
nodes.rationale: The lock is the first movement of money and the preimage reveal IS the acknowledgment, so settlement and acknowledgment are atomic; no claim before the timelock refunds and opens an exception.

nodes.label: Payment flow (O1-O8, P1-P12)
nodes.rationale: Supersedes the payment sequence in architecture.md §4.1. No pre-established payer-payee link is required: B2B reality is paying an invoice from a supplier you have never paid, and forcing a two-sided link first is a chicken-and-egg problem for no gain, because the identity binding rather than the relationship defeats a tampered address.

nodes.label: B1 Hedera ATS track
nodes.rationale: On-chain deployment is re-verified by a read-only suite against the public mirror node so a judge can run it without a key, and created_timestamp matching catches a swapped contract rather than only a missing one. The remaining gap is a funded Hedera account, so the API still resolves complianceGateway mock.

nodes.label: PaymentHtlc.sol
nodes.rationale: No partial claims, no multi-hop, no cross-chain. Claim is restricted to the payee and closed once the timelock passes so claim and refund never overlap; refund is callable by anyone but funds only ever go to the recorded payer. The escrow itself is granted KYC, because the compliance gate applies to contracts too.

nodes.label: D39 priority change — Hedera ATS is the primary deliverable
nodes.norm_label: d39 priority change — hedera ats is the primary deliverable
nodes.rationale: Every B1 qualification bar must be met because partial credit is worth nothing there; Track A is the credibility behind the submission, not the submission itself.

nodes.label: DigiLockerProvider (India, Sandbox aggregator)
nodes.rationale: The human consent step cannot be automated, and that is the point — it is what makes DigiLocker legally defensible as an identity source. One consent flow satisfies legal identity + address + photo + tax ID at once, reaching TIER3_ADDRESS in a single step, so the postcard path is unnecessary for India.

nodes.label: IdentityProvider interface
nodes.rationale: Pluggable so non-India payees fall through to a generic provider — the same pattern as VendorMatcher.

nodes.label: MockIdentityProvider (fixture replay)
nodes.rationale: Live KYC calls are billed per request, so development replays a recorded capture. Mock mode must still walk created -> succeeded via a local stub page rather than short-circuiting, or bugs in the polling path go uncaught.

nodes.label: Onboarding O1-O8
nodes.rationale: O2, O4 and O7 prove who, key possession, and personhood/continuity respectively; none substitutes for another.

nodes.label: Check 2 — cross-document consistency
nodes.rationale: Name, dob and gender disagreement between Aadhaar and PAN is a strong fraud signal and must block CONFIRMED.

nodes.label: Two fixture tiers (real gitignored, synthetic committed)
nodes.norm_label: two fixture tiers (real gitignored, synthetic committed)
nodes.rationale: Redaction is impossible: editing one byte of the signed XML invalidates the XMLDSig signature, so there is no redacted-but-valid variant. index.json doubles as the test oracle and is read at runtime rather than hardcoded, because the expected values identify a real person.

nodes.label: Identity-to-wallet binding (EIP-712 IdentityBinding)
nodes.rationale: DigiLocker proves who someone is and EIP-712 proves what key they hold; neither alone maps identity to a wallet. The signed attestation turns a data-entry claim into a repudiation-resistant act by the payee, usable in recovery proceedings.

nodes.label: Mandatory format normalisation before comparison
nodes.rationale: The same person's details come back formatted three different ways across endpoints (19/11/2001 vs 19-11-2001; male/M/MALE; mixed-case names), so naive equality rejects a legitimate user — the single most likely bug in the integration. The profile date_of_birth is documented as unix-ms but returned DD/MM/YYYY live, so both types must be handled.

nodes.label: Swappable dependencies behind interfaces
nodes.rationale: IdentityProvider / VendorMatcher / SanctionsScreener are resolved only in api/src/container.ts. Three of four external integrations are access-gated, so the interfaces are why Phases 1-3 are not blocked on any of them.

nodes.label: deployReceivable factory deploy
nodes.rationale: Factory deploy for a verified invoice.

nodes.label: Identity module and the four checks
nodes.norm_label: identity module and the four checks
nodes.rationale: Holds providers, the four checks, normalisation and parsers together because normalisation is what makes the checks meaningful against inconsistently formatted upstream data.

nodes.label: internal identity-registry hook
nodes.rationale: Exposed under modules/internal/ specifically for consumption by the Hedera ATS Control List, making platform KYC state the compliance source of truth for the token.

nodes.label: Three-way format inconsistency (date, gender, name case)
nodes.norm_label: three-way format inconsistency (date, gender, name case)
nodes.rationale: The same person's details are formatted three different ways across endpoints (profile DD/MM/YYYY vs XML DD-MM-YYYY; male / M / MALE; Aadhaar title case vs PAN all caps). Normalise before comparing or the cross-document consistency check falsely rejects a legitimate user.

nodes.label: Control List module
nodes.rationale: Points at GET /internal/identity-registry/:address in @cp/api — the real integration point.

nodes.label: @cp/contracts
nodes.rationale: Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio integration. Verify SDK method signatures against the installed package version before wiring — §4.5 gives conceptual shape, not verified signatures.

nodes.label: KYC data as ERC-3643 compliance backend
nodes.norm_label: kyc data as erc-3643 compliance backend
nodes.rationale: Wiring the Control List to the platform's identity registry makes this platform's KYC data the compliance backend ERC-3643 actually calls out to, rather than a cosmetic add-on.

nodes.label: Clear Signing on-device confirmation
nodes.rationale: The confirm/reject decision happens on the physical device screen; the CLI prompt is a convenience, not the security boundary.

nodes.label: wallet-cli execa wrapper
nodes.rationale: Wraps @ledgerhq/wallet-cli and blocks until the device responds, so the blocking call is the signing gate.

nodes.label: Ledger AI tools and CLI docs
nodes.norm_label: ledger ai tools and cli docs

nodes.label: Ledger device-app and Ledger OS docs
nodes.norm_label: ledger device-app and ledger os docs

nodes.label: Ledger developer docs URL index
nodes.rationale: A flat 320-URL crawl of developers.ledger.com kept in-repo as a reference index for the hardware-wallet integration work.

nodes.label: Speculos transport switch
nodes.rationale: WALLET_CLI_TRANSPORT=speculos changes only the transport target; the code path stays identical, so a Speculos demo exercises the real flow.

nodes.label: XMLDSig signatures from UIDAI and Income Tax Department
nodes.norm_label: xmldsig signatures from uidai and income tax department

nodes.label: Synthetic DigiLocker fixture tier
nodes.rationale: The committed tier of fake identities with unsigned or self-signed XML; it is what CI and UI work run against. Not yet populated.

nodes.label: Aadhaar last-4 display only
nodes.rationale: Aadhaar is only ever shown as last-4 and no input may accept a full Aadhaar number, because receiving one creates Data Vault obligations this flow is designed to avoid (§3).

nodes.label: Two-tier fixture strategy
nodes.rationale: It is real-and-secret or synthetic-and-unsigned; there is no redacted middle ground that still validates, because editing one byte of a signed XML invalidates the XMLDSig signature. Hence a gitignored real tier for signature tests and a committed synthetic tier for CI and UI.

nodes.label: Deliberately preserved format gotchas
nodes.rationale: The synthetic set is worthless if it is internally tidy: reproduce the three real-capture inconsistencies (date DD/MM/YYYY vs DD-MM-YYYY plus a unix-ms variant, gender male/M/MALE, name title vs upper case) or the normalisation layer will pass CI and fail on live data.

nodes.label: Test CA root for synthetic signatures
nodes.norm_label: test ca root for synthetic signatures
nodes.rationale: Signature verification against the real UIDAI chain belongs to the real tier only. Synthetic index.json should expect xmlSignatureVerified: false under the real CA root; tests needing true must use a test root the synthetic documents are signed against.

nodes.label: Biometric stays inside World ID (D49)
nodes.rationale: World never returns the face: no name, no document, no image, no facial template reaches this platform.

nodes.label: Nullifier as scoped pseudonym
nodes.rationale: A one-way, RP- and action-scoped pseudonym: it cannot be reversed to a person and is meaningless outside our rp_id, which is why these fixtures carry no identity data and can be committed.

nodes.label: Nullifier continuity property
nodes.rationale: Capture 02 has a different nonce, merkle_root and proof bytes from capture 01 yet the same nullifier — proving same human, same action, same nullifier, forever, which is what the onboarding-to-approval design depends on (see D49a).

nodes.label: UNIQUE (nullifier, action, signal) constraint
nodes.rationale: Database-level backstop: proof reuse is caught regardless of application logic.

nodes.label: Medium-assurance copy constraint
nodes.rationale: Selfie Check is medium assurance, so copy must say "a live human confirmed this action", never "identity verified" (§4.6). Overclaiming the assurance level in UI text is a compliance defect, not a wording preference.

nodes.label: Empty-signal proof binding
nodes.rationale: The committed proofs are genuine ZK proofs but bound to the empty signal, while every gate requires a proof bound to a specific signal checked server-side — so they cannot be replayed for anything that matters. If a capture is ever taken with a real signal against production, re-evaluate before committing.

nodes.label: CRE TEE workflow handler and VendorMatcher adapter
nodes.norm_label: cre tee workflow handler and vendormatcher adapter

nodes.label: Unused-but-required RPC configuration
nodes.rationale: The workflow does not read or write a chain — its result is the HTTP trigger's synchronous response, not an on-chain report — but simulate still requires at least one RPC under the target because the simulator's runtime initializes chain clients unconditionally (confirmed by the error "no RPC URLs found for target"). Extend only if a future revision writes on-chain via usingTheDons().

nodes.label: Vault DON secrets on the mainnet registry
nodes.norm_label: vault don secrets on the mainnet registry
nodes.rationale: Vault DON secrets live on the mainnet registry even for a staging workflow; without an ethereum-mainnet RPC the secrets commands stop on an interactive "responses cannot be validated" prompt — the CLI correctly refusing to trust a gateway reply it cannot check against the chain. Supplying the RPC is supplying the check, not skipping it.

nodes.label: cre workflow simulate is not a security demonstration
nodes.norm_label: cre workflow simulate is not a security demonstration
nodes.rationale: simulate verifies logic only. It is not a real enclave and must never be cited as a security demonstration (§4.4).

nodes.label: Adapted workflow artifact paths
nodes.rationale: Paths verified against a real `cre init --template=hello-confidential-workflows-ts` scaffold and adapted from its flat layout: this file sits two levels below the package root, so secrets-path reaches back up to ../../secrets.yaml alongside project.yaml.

nodes.label: private deployment-registry choice
nodes.rationale: "private" is Chainlink-hosted and off-chain: no gas and no wallet key, which is what a demo deployment wants. The alternative shown by `cre registry list`, "onchain:ethereum-mainnet", needs both.

nodes.label: Local DigiLocker consent stub page
nodes.rationale: Serves IDENTITY_PROVIDER=mock (§4.7.1): human consent is the one step that cannot be mocked meaningfully, so a local page flips the session to succeeded and keeps the state machine honest.

nodes.label: index.json expected_check_results oracle
nodes.rationale: Values live only in the gitignored index.json and are read at runtime by apps/api/test/fixtures/oracle.ts rather than hardcoded into tests, because they identify a real person.

nodes.label: MockIdentityProvider fixture replayer
nodes.rationale: Reads index.json, matches on method + path, returns the fixture body, and serves documents/*.xml in place of the presigned URL, so the provider seam is the only thing that changes between mock and live.

nodes.label: Short-lived presigned document URLs
nodes.rationale: Document URLs in live responses expire within minutes: download immediately, never persist the URL. Fixture values are marked SYNTHETIC for the same reason tokens are — credentials and expiring URLs do not belong in a fixture.

nodes.label: DIGILOCKER_FIXTURE_DIR switch
nodes.rationale: The synthetic tier must mirror the real tier's layout exactly so MockIdentityProvider can point at either directory with no code change.

nodes.label: index.json known_gotchas oracle
nodes.rationale: index.json states what a correct implementation must conclude; four of the five gotchas are traps that fail silently, so it must be read before writing anything against the fixtures.

nodes.label: Ledger Clear Signing on-device confirmation
nodes.rationale: The confirm/reject happens on the physical device screen and the CLI call blocks until the device responds, so the recipient and amount a human sees are the ones actually signed.

nodes.label: apps/approval-bridge
nodes.rationale: Runs on the approver's local machine, never cloud infra, because it is the only process with USB access to the Ledger. The device transport is an env var so the code path stays identical for USB and Speculos.

nodes.label: Principle 1 — the agent never holds a private key
nodes.norm_label: principle 1 — the agent never holds a private key
nodes.rationale: Autonomous code only writes proposals to a queue; only a human-triggered process gated by Ledger hardware confirmation can move funds.

nodes.label: agent / approver role separation at the API layer
nodes.norm_label: agent / approver role separation at the api layer
nodes.rationale: The literal implementation of principle 1: separate keys per role enforced in middleware rather than the UI, with a test asserting an agent-scoped token is refused on /approvals/*.

nodes.label: Principle 5 — signing and read-only are separate processes
nodes.norm_label: principle 5 — signing and read-only are separate processes
nodes.rationale: Architectural separation, not just separate code paths, so a bug in the read path cannot reach a key.

nodes.label: Open gap: nothing broadcasts a transfer
nodes.norm_label: open gap: nothing broadcasts a transfer
nodes.rationale: apps/approval-bridge/src/wallet-cli.ts stops at 'Local broadcast is not wired yet' — it signs nothing and sends nothing, so the recorded HTLC lock describes a movement something else must have made.

nodes.label: approval-bridge is a separate app, not a module
nodes.norm_label: approval-bridge is a separate app, not a module
nodes.rationale: Signing and read-only must be separate processes, not separate code paths in one process (design principle 5); collapsing them for convenience destroys the boundary.

nodes.label: P5 payee challenge triggers (risk-based)
nodes.rationale: Detects a stolen key: a thief can sign the consent and claim the funds but cannot produce the nullifier. Enrolment at O7 is what matters — it makes the challenge available the moment something looks wrong.

nodes.label: Principle 2 — no raw PII on-chain, commitment hashes only
nodes.norm_label: principle 2 — no raw pii on-chain, commitment hashes only
nodes.rationale: On-chain data is permanent and public and encryption does not fix that, so only fixed-size commitment hashes go on-chain and raw data stays off-chain, encrypted.

nodes.label: World ID nullifier never written to the chain
nodes.norm_label: world id nullifier never written to the chain
nodes.rationale: The nullifier is a stable per-person identifier within an action, so publishing it would let anyone holding two records link the same human across payments.

nodes.label: The PII rule for evidence payloads
nodes.norm_label: the pii rule for evidence payloads
nodes.rationale: Every field must be an identifier, an enum, a score or a hash — that is the test to apply before adding one.

nodes.label: Known residual: the one-bit leak
nodes.rationale: Irreducible for any check that decides whether to pay; throttled rather than eliminated because every probe needs the target to actively accept a payment request and generates a mismatch alert, so twenty probes is twenty prompts to one person who then blocks the sender.

nodes.label: Row-level security on every public table (D46)
nodes.norm_label: row-level security on every public table (d46)
nodes.rationale: The database was wide open through Supabase's REST API — every table readable and UPDATE/DELETE permitted with only the publishable key, a key designed to ship in browsers. Re-asserted by a migration looping over pg_tables so a table added later cannot miss it.
